note: The Romans arrested Rabbi Elazar ben Perata on five charges and Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon on one. Hanina told Elazar he would be saved, because he had done acts of kindness as well as study Torah, while Hanina would not. At his trial Elazar denied teaching Torah and stealing, and miracles backed him: hornets showed which wool was warp and which woof, and an old man was trampled at the house of Abidan that day, as he said he feared. When a man rose to testify that he had freed his slave, Elijah flung a letter the man carried four hundred parasangs, and the man went after it and never came back. Hanina, asked why he taught Torah, said 'As the Lord my God commanded me.' He was sentenced to burning, his wife to execution, his daughter to a brothel.
why: The Gemara returns to the Sages tried by the Romans. Along the way it uses Hanina's words to teach, with Rav Huna, that Torah study without acts of kindness is not enough, and it explains what each of the three had done to deserve their sentence.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata
people.about: A Sage arrested by the Romans on five charges, who is saved through a series of miracles.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage arrested for teaching Torah in public, sentenced to burning; the Gemara says he pronounced God's name in public.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as a Roman nobleman to stop a witness against Rabbi Elazar ben Perata.

terms.meaning: The two sets of threads in weaving: the warp is stretched on the loom and the woof is passed through it. An expert weaver can tell them apart.
A meeting place where debates on wisdom and faith were held, which the Romans expected Rabbi Elazar ben Perata to attend.
God's proper name, which by tradition is not pronounced as it is written.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly four kilometers; four hundred of them is a very great distance.

note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was walking, leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, and told him: you missed the study hall last night, when we permitted the oil of gentiles. Simlai replied that in their days he would permit gentiles' bread as well. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia answered that people would then call them a permissive court, as they had called Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer 'Yosef the Permissive' for his three lenient rulings. Simlai pointed out that Yosei had permitted three things, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia only one, so another would make just two. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said he had already permitted another: according to Shmuel, it was his court that allowed a woman to remarry under a certain conditional bill of divorce.
why: The exchange is the Gemara's record that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court permitted gentiles' oil; the Gemara then turns aside to examine that same court's ruling on the conditional bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The head of the court that permitted the oil of gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's attendant, who was absent from the study hall the night the oil was permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer of Tzereida
people.about: An earlier Sage nicknamed 'Yosef the Permissive' for three lenient rulings.

terms.meaning: Olive oil made by non-Jews, which had been forbidden to Jews until this court permitted it.
The document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was given on a condition, and the husband died before the condition could be tested.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings on which the Gemara comments.

note: Rav Ashi came to a certain place where he was served a fish that looked like a shefarnuna. He put it in a white vessel, saw the scales it shed, and permitted it. Rabba bar bar Hana came to Akra DeAgma and was served tzahanta, a dish of small fish, and heard a man call it batei, the name of a non-kosher sea creature. He concluded there was something non-kosher in it and did not eat. In the morning he examined the dish, found a non-kosher substance in it, and applied to himself the verse: 'No sin shall befall the righteous.'
why: The Gemara is gathering cases of Sages deciding whether an unfamiliar fish was kosher, mostly by looking for scales; Rabba bar bar Hana's case adds a different kind of evidence, a name overheard at the table.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who checks a doubtful fish for scales and permits it.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who refuses a dish because of what a man called it, and turns out to be right.

terms.meaning: A fish is kosher only if it has fins and scales, so finding scales settles whether a doubtful fish may be eaten.
A kind of fish the Gemara has just called permitted.
Food that Jewish law forbids to be eaten.

note: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda taught that one may not make even a wooden candelabrum like the Temple's, as the Hasmoneans made one of wood. The Rabbis answered that the Hasmoneans' candelabrum was not wood: its branches were iron spits covered with tin. When they grew richer they made it of silver, and when they grew richer still, of gold.
why: Abaye cites this teaching for his view that the Torah bans making only copies that can truly reproduce their model, such as a seven-branched candelabrum, which is why figures of the moon were allowed.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who holds that even a wooden copy of the Temple candelabrum is forbidden.

terms.meaning: The seven-branched lampstand (menorah) that stood in the Temple. A private copy with seven lamps is forbidden.
The family of priests who ruled Judea and purified the Temple; the text says they first had to make the candelabrum from poor materials.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
